en: There is a shrine where a saint passed;
My dear foal,
You will pay your respects as you go.
When you go beyond it,
Even a brave man's thoughts are troubled:
Wild asses play in its sands,
The plain of lower Kazy-Kurt.
Do not turn to the left;
Do not leave the right-hand side.
When you go beyond it,
There is the pale, misty grassy slope,
The broad valley stretching back—
That is the land of Oluya-Ata.
When you reach Oluya-Ata,
If you look to the west,
Kara-Balta and Sokuluk,
Their ridges appear dimly.
When you see them,
My son, your heart will be deeply troubled.
If you turn right, my orphan,
A gray neck of land like a saddle-back,
That is the pass called Jorgo.
I, your bereaved, ill-fated mother,
That is where I crossed in grief.
Climb that saddle-backed neck of land,
My orphan, climb it.
When you look beyond,
Separate patches of land will appear;
Rounded passes will appear.
Foothill after foothill will appear;
A hilly, ridge-filled pass will appear.
That is tamarisk-covered Keng-Kol,
Kumys by day, girls by night,
Those are the joyful Kyrgyz people.
Parted from that people,
I am your mother who wandered desolate!
And, orphan, listen:
The place where my fortress came to grief,
Where they joined in plundering my goods,
Where the six scoundrels took their fill.
If you turn and look,
May I take your misfortune upon me,
There are the foothills of Uch-Koshoy.
There is no end to telling
Your mother Kanykey's grief.
If what I say is not false,
If your impetuous widowed mother
Has not been struck by misfortune,
If her good fortune has not fled,
If your poor mother has not grown confused,
When you reach Uch-Koshoy,
My orphan, who knows? I do not know; it is hard.
From a plain where no soul wanders,
My orphan, something will appear before you,
Well known and proven among the people,
If you recognize its worth, my orphan,
An inheritance left by your father Khan Manas.
To a person without ritual ablution,
Kumayyk will not appear;
To an ill-natured person,
Kumayyk will not be found.
Encountered by mystery,
In the desert of Mediyan,
Your father traveled five days,
Came upon water,
And where he performed his ablutions,
At Kum-Bulak itself,
Beside the great God,
On the great hill itself,
On a Thursday,
On Friday's blessed night,
Encountered by mystery,
For your father who has gone to the hereafter,
It was found in that place.
For your father visited by Khyzyr,
Thus the mighty ones were found.
For your father who offered sacrifice to Baabedin,
All the heroes were encountered.
Take heed, orphan, understand:
A gray puppy the size of a fist,
Thus Kumayyk was found:
He was raw flesh born of a gray vulture,
Before his eyes had opened,
He was found for your fierce khan father.
Ajybay of the Argyn khan,
Your father's companion,
Bakay, the most excellent of heroes,
Your father's companion in the next world,
When they found the fist-sized gray puppy,
When they found Kumayyk,
When they found the gray puppy,
They named him mighty Kumayyk.
For his feast, Khan Bakay
Slaughtered nine gray mares.
He continued from the old tales;
Bakay asked of what he knew.
Khan Bakay, born a leopard,
Dispelled all sorrow.
For fierce Manas the leopard's
Good fortune he was found;
They named him mighty Kumayyk.
“If such service is not done,
Valiant Manas, listen!
It will be a fault, they used to say.
If words do not sully him,
If Kumayyk remains so,
He will vanish, they used to say.
Dwelling in every mountain,
A hidden spirit will nurture him, they used to say.
One who has committed no adultery or sin,
One pure among women,
A wife will nurture him, they used to say, Manas!”
Khan Bakay and Manas conferred;
Bakay found the answer.
“Manas, have you seen what I have seen?
Have you perceived what I have perceived?
I saw a land like broad Bukhara;
I saw a stately, hapless man.
In Bukhara I saw Khan Temir;
I saw a soul of saintly birth.
She is the beauty among the dusky-complexioned,
The radiant one among Muslims.
Among women, more skillful than a spearman,
The finest of womankind.
She would join what had broken,
Gather what had scattered.
She is a Night of Power;
She is a slave girl like a saint.
She is the craftswoman among women;
She is Khan Temir's daughter in Bukhara.
She is still a little girl;
Her age has not passed fourteen.
Loading eighty camels with gold coins,
Let us go to Khan Temir.
‘I have chosen her; give me your daughter,’ we shall say,
And go and place the betrothal earrings.
If God grants it, let us have
Kanykey raise the mighty one.
This mighty Kumayyk's
Unless Kanykey raises him,
No other woman will know his ways.”
Traveling by night, not by day,
Yet traveling by day without losing hope,
Crossing chest upon chest of mountain passes,
Traveling the land along Samarkand,
Your father Khan Manas,
With Ajybay and Bakay,
When they went to broad Bukhara,
Loading eighty camels with gold coins,
Your father Manas the leopard,
When he came to seek betrothal with me,
When they put betrothal earrings on me,
When they bound me to marriage,
I was still a little girl,
My hair not yet long enough to braid,
I, your unfortunate mother,
Then a beauty among women,
A maiden of fourteen.
When your wolf-maned father came,
Manas the leopard, towering proudly,
Pressed me more and more,
A gray pup the size of a fist,
Whose eyes had not yet opened,
Your father, Khan Manas,
Gave to me, your wretched mother.
Your khan father Manas swore an oath,
He made a solemn promise:
“If you raise Kumaik for me,
I shall surely show you every care;
Throughout all the lands within my reach,
I shall make you queen.
I shall not lay a whip across you,
Nor take another wife to rival you.
I shall not show my baser nature,
Nor let a harsh word touch you.
Neglectful care will bring disgrace;
Kumaik is entrusted to you.
Hang an amulet about his neck,
Take good care of Kumaik.
If you care badly for my dog,
You will see the foolishness
Of your husband, wolf-maned Manas.
If I, Manas, remain alive,
And this Kumaik here—
If you take poor care of him,
This very Bukhara's
Treasures I shall plunder.
For this dog Kumaik,
I shall wreak great havoc.”
Your father often said this;
When he came walking slowly,
The gray pup the size of a fist
He handed over as a sacred trust,
Giving it to me, your wretched mother.
When I took it in my hands and looked,
It had little prospect of surviving.
If the hound were carelessly raised,
Bringing black night upon my wretched head,
It was likely to die.
“My resources will utterly fail,” I thought,
“Our deaths will come together,” I thought.
“If this pup is left untended,
It will starve to death,” I thought.
I fed it milk from my mouth;
Thus I raised the hound.
I fed it meat with my hand,
I spent my days in anxious care.
Without recoiling in disgust,
I made my tongue a teat.
I levied tribute upon Bukhara
And had a young mare slaughtered.
The young mare's sweet rib fat
I cut away with my teeth,
And let it suck from my tongue;
Thus I raised the hound.
Without resting on my elbow,
Without a moment's sleep,
Thus I raised the hound.
Without rest throughout the day,
Without sleep throughout the night,
Thus I raised the hound.
Winter passed and spring arrived;
My wits wandered, my strength failed.
Fanged beasts were deadly enemies of the hound.
At my father Temir Khan's great court,
I had a pit of forty ells dug.
I had Kumaik placed inside;
Forty hunters from Bukhara—
Over Kumaik
I had them stand guard.
Keeping lions from seizing him,
That Kumaik you have seen,
Keeping him from needless death,
I barely managed to preserve him.
When six full months had passed,
The Kumaik I was raising,
When the time came to prowl,
Would bite and fight even a tiger.
When the time came to play,
He proved a blazing ember;
No fanged beast was so unruly.
The steel collar around his neck
He bit and tore apart.
I, your unfortunate, luckless mother—
Before I could cry out and protect him,
Into the saxaul embers
He struck his tail.
His tail touched the coals;
Two fingerbreadths of it were burned.
God had taken away my sense.
That day your valiant, princely father,
Furious and looming proudly,
His nose bulging like a leather flask,
Arrived on a bridegroom's visit.
Inspecting Kumaik,
He saw the tail and raised a quarrel,
